Timeline::period_start¶

Back to Timeline API Reference

Signature¶

Timeline Timeline::period_start(std::string_view unit) const

Find The Beginning Of Each Containing Time Unit¶

period_start() replaces every defined instant with the first instant of the local calendar unit that contains it. It answers questions such as “when did this value’s month begin?” and “which local hour contains this event?” while remaining a Timeline operation: the result still contains exact instants, not labels, interval objects, or integer group identifiers.

This is useful when an instant is needed as a canonical boundary. Values that belong to the same month, for example, receive the same month-start instant and can then be compared or used as lower bounds. If the intended result is a calendar component such as the number 7, use month() instead. If the intended result is a distance between two values, use span() or diff().

The accepted units are deliberately narrow and canonical:

unit

Retained local fields

Fields reset to their beginning

"year"

year

month and day become January 1; clock becomes midnight

"month"

year and month

day becomes 1; clock becomes midnight

"day"

year, month, and day

clock becomes midnight

"hour"

date and hour

minute, second, and fraction become zero

"minute"

date, hour, and minute

second and fraction become zero

"second"

date, hour, minute, and second

fractional nanoseconds become zero

Matching is ASCII case-insensitive, so "YEAR" and "year" name the same unit. Abbreviations and plural spellings are not aliases: "Y", "min", and "years" are rejected. One vocabulary avoids ambiguous call sites and keeps configuration text consistent with the named Timeline methods.

Example 1: See Every Boundary From One Instant¶

The source below is noon in Edmonton during daylight-saving time. Each call works from the displayed local calendar, not by truncating the stored UTC nanoseconds.

const auto value = pluss::timeline::make(
    "2024-07-15T18:34:56.123456789Z")
    .tz_convert("America/Edmonton");

auto show = [](std::string_view label, const pluss::Timeline& result) {
  std::cout << "\n=== " << label << " ===\n"
            << pluss::note::print(
                   pluss::timeline::format(result, "%FT%T.%f%z"))
            << '\n';
};

show("source", value);
show("year", value.period_start("year"));
show("month", value.period_start("month"));
show("day", value.period_start("day"));
show("hour", value.period_start("hour"));
show("minute", value.period_start("minute"));
show("second", value.period_start("second"));

Output¶

=== source ===
Note(shape=[], dim=0, numel=1, encoding=utf8)
"2024-07-15T12:34:56.123456789-06:00"

=== year ===
Note(shape=[], dim=0, numel=1, encoding=utf8)
"2024-01-01T00:00:00.000000000-07:00"

=== month ===
Note(shape=[], dim=0, numel=1, encoding=utf8)
"2024-07-01T00:00:00.000000000-06:00"

=== day ===
Note(shape=[], dim=0, numel=1, encoding=utf8)
"2024-07-15T00:00:00.000000000-06:00"

=== hour ===
Note(shape=[], dim=0, numel=1, encoding=utf8)
"2024-07-15T12:00:00.000000000-06:00"

=== minute ===
Note(shape=[], dim=0, numel=1, encoding=utf8)
"2024-07-15T12:34:00.000000000-06:00"

=== second ===
Note(shape=[], dim=0, numel=1, encoding=utf8)
"2024-07-15T12:34:56.000000000-06:00"

The year boundary uses -07:00, while the July boundaries use -06:00. period_start() preserves the timezone and the requested civil boundary; it does not preserve the source’s numeric UTC offset when the boundary belongs to a different offset season.

Local Boundaries, Not Elapsed Buckets¶

For timezone-aware values, every unit is resolved in tz(). A day starts at local midnight even when the elapsed distance from the preceding midnight is 23 or 25 hours. Year and month starts are reconstructed from local calendar fields. Day through second starts use local wall-clock flooring.

This makes period_start("day") a calendar operation. It is not equivalent to dividing epoch nanoseconds by 86,400 seconds, which would create UTC-aligned buckets and assign the wrong local date in many timezones.

Applying the same unit twice is idempotent in value:

const auto once = value.period_start("month");
const auto twice = once.period_start("month");
std::cout << "\n=== idempotent ===\n"
          << std::boolalpha << once.eq(twice).all().item<bool>() << '\n';

Output¶

=== idempotent ===
true

The method is nevertheless out-of-place. It allocates a result and leaves the receiver unchanged, even when every input already lies on the requested boundary.

Example 2: Shape, NaT, Leap Dates, And Pre-Epoch Values¶

Projection is elementwise and shape-preserving. NaT remains NaT; it is not interpreted as an old date and does not make neighboring lanes fail.

const auto matrix = pluss::timeline::make({
    {"2024-02-29T23:59:59.999999999Z", ""},
    {"1969-12-31T23:59:59.500000000Z", "2025-01-01T00:00:00Z"},
});

std::cout << pluss::note::print(pluss::timeline::format(
    matrix.period_start("month"), "%FT%T.%f%z")) << '\n';

Output¶

Note(shape=[2, 2], dim=2, numel=4, encoding=utf8)
[
  ["2024-02-01T00:00:00.000000000+00:00", "NaT"], 
  ["1969-12-01T00:00:00.000000000+00:00", "2025-01-01T00:00:00.000000000+00:00"]
]

Leap-day input does not require a special policy because the result is the first day of February. Negative epoch values use mathematical calendar boundaries, so the December 1969 lane stays in December rather than being truncated toward the Unix epoch.

Example 3: Repeated Local Hours Retain Their Identity¶

When clocks move backward, one wall-clock hour occurs twice. Flooring either occurrence must retain which occurrence contained the source instant.

const auto folds = pluss::timeline::make({
    "2024-11-03T07:45:00Z",
    "2024-11-03T08:45:00Z",
}).tz_convert("America/Edmonton");

std::cout << pluss::note::print(pluss::timeline::format(
    folds.period_start("hour"), "%FT%T.%f%z")) << '\n';

Output¶

Note(shape=[2], dim=1, numel=2, encoding=utf8)
["2024-11-03T01:00:00.000000000-06:00", "2024-11-03T01:00:00.000000000-07:00"]

Both results display 01:00, but they remain different instants because their offsets differ. This distinction is preserved in ticks(), comparisons, and later elapsed-time arithmetic.

Example 4: Non-Contiguous Input Uses Logical Order¶

period_start() accepts the same strided Timeline storage as the rest of the public surface. It reads logical lanes through their strides and returns a contiguous owning result.

auto storage = pluss::timeline::make({
    "2024-01-15T12:00:00Z", "2030-01-01T00:00:00Z",
    "2024-03-20T18:00:00Z", "2030-01-01T00:00:00Z",
}).ticks();
const std::array<std::int64_t, 1> sizes{2};
const std::array<std::int64_t, 1> strides{2};
const auto strided = pluss::Timeline::from_buffer(
    storage.data(), sizes, strides, {}, "UTC");

std::cout << pluss::note::print(pluss::timeline::format(
    strided.period_start("year"), "%FT%T.%f%z")) << '\n';

Output¶

Note(shape=[2], dim=1, numel=2, encoding=utf8)
["2024-01-01T00:00:00.000000000+00:00", "2024-01-01T00:00:00.000000000+00:00"]

The two interleaved 2030 storage positions are not part of the logical view.

Example 5: Empty Shapes Remain Empty¶

const auto empty = pluss::timeline::from_epoch(
    std::vector<std::int64_t>{}, {2, 0});
std::cout << pluss::note::print(pluss::timeline::format(
    empty.period_start("day"), "%FT%T.%f%z")) << '\n';

Output¶

Note(shape=[2, 0], dim=2, numel=0, encoding=utf8)
[]

The rank and zero extent are retained. Unit validation still occurs before element traversal, so an unsupported unit throws even for an empty Timeline.

Example 6: Invalid And Removed Spellings Fail Clearly¶

const auto value = pluss::timeline::make("2024-07-15T18:34:56Z");

try {
  (void)value.period_start("years");
} catch (const pluss::Error&) {
  std::cout << "\n=== plural_alias ===\nrejected\n";
}
try {
  (void)value.period_start("week");
} catch (const pluss::Error&) {
  std::cout << "\n=== unsupported_unit ===\nrejected\n";
}

Output¶

=== plural_alias ===
rejected

=== unsupported_unit ===
rejected

"years" demonstrates that plural compatibility aliases are intentionally absent. "week" is not supported because a week boundary requires an explicit weekday convention; this method does not silently choose one.

Timezone lookup and local-boundary resolution can also throw when timezone metadata is invalid or when a requested boundary cannot be represented as an epoch-nanosecond instant. No partial result is returned.

Choosing A Neighboring Operation¶

  • Use floor for second-through-day flooring when its compact unit vocabulary is already appropriate at the call site.

  • Use date when the request is specifically local midnight for each value’s date.

  • Use year, month, or another field projection when the result should be an integer component rather than a boundary instant.

  • Use shift to move values by units instead of locating the beginning of their current unit.

  • Use span or diff to measure between two Timelines.
